title: Lower the gaze
hook: believing men and women are both told to lower their gaze and guard their modesty (24:30–31)

segments.voice: Yesterday: husn al-zann, choosing the good guess. Your line was think well first.

A face across the train car. A stranger's phone screen, lit up and readable. A photo that stops the thumb mid-scroll. The eyes move first, before anyone has decided anything, and then they linger. Advertisers know this, and so does every app built to keep a thumb scrolling. Surah An-Nur gives a short instruction about the eyes. It is often remembered as a rule for women alone. Look at who hears it first.

Verse thirty. Pickthall: "Tell the believing men to lower their gaze and be modest." Men first. Then the next verse turns to women with the same opening: "And tell the believing women to lower their gaze and be modest". Same verbs, same duty. The verse to women goes on with more detail about dress, and scholars have written a great deal about that. But the gaze comes first, and it's shared. The Arabic is yaghuddu min absarihim. Ghadd means to lower, to lessen, the way you'd lower your voice. And the little word min, from, matters. Some commentators read it as: lower some of your gaze. Not shut your eyes, not walk around staring at your shoes. You still see the person you're talking to. What gets lowered is the lingering, the second look that turns into staring. A hadith in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi makes the same point. The Prophet ﷺ told 'Ali: don't follow one glance with another. The first is yours; the second is not. The first look just happens. The second is a choice. And it isn't only about attraction. In a hadith in Bukhari, the Prophet listed the rights of the road for people who sit by the street, and lowering the gaze is the first of them. Next to it: not harming anyone, returning greetings, encouraging good. So guarding the eyes is also manners: not staring into the neighbor's open door, not reading a stranger's messages over their shoulder, not lingering on someone who'd rather not be looked at.
screen: `MEN ADDRESSED FIRST.` · `GHADD: LOWER, LESSEN.` · `THE FIRST LOOK IS YOURS.` · `A RIGHT OF THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Lower your gaze gently toward the floor in front of you, not closed, just softened, and notice how often your eyes want to move. Each time they do, let them come back. Keep the first look, and let the second one go.
Ghadd al-basar. Lowering the gaze: keep the first look, let go of the second. Said first to men, then to women.
Your line: guard the eyes. The first look happens; the second is a choice. That's day four hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Many Muslims understand lowering the gaze as avoiding lingering or immodest looks, for men and women alike, and some extend it to what they choose to watch online.

fork.reveal: lowering the gaze comes first in Bukhari's report, then not causing harm, returning greetings and encouraging good.

original.note: Arabic: lowering the gaze; ghadd is to lower or lessen, basar is sight.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rule for women about where to look.
what it means: a shared duty, men first, to lower the lingering second look, and part of everyday manners too.
what a scholar hears: the partitive min in 'yaghuddu min absarihim'; the hadith to 'Ali (Abu Dawud 2149, Tirmidhi 2777); the rights of the road (Bukhari 2465).
recall: a favor, a blessing, a grace
